A name that matches nothing names the closest ones and the tool that lists them; an archived channel is said to be archived, and that it can be read but not posted in; a draft already where a new one would go is quoted; a message too long for the server says its length and the server's limit. A failure Mattermost reports is passed on with its status and id, which is how the model tells a missing permission from a missing thing.

Lists are bounded: each list tool has a small default and a hard maximum, and says when it cut something off. A tool's description says what it is for and how it behaves, including what it refuses and, on a server set to ask, that it asks; each argument is described in the input schema, and the description repeats neither the arguments nor an example call, which every session would pay for.

A model asks for things by the names a person uses, and guesses ids badly. A person pastes what Mattermost shows them, which is a link; asked where something was said, a model that has only ids links the conversation, a direct message's whole history, rather than the post. An error that says only "not found" leaves it to guess again; one that names the closest match ends the guessing in one call. Matching a part of a name helps only until it is ambiguous, and an ambiguous name resolved silently posts to the wrong channel, so ambiguity is refused rather than settled by a rule the person never sees.

docs.title: Not chosen
docs.text:
• Check a post's destination against a display name the model passes, as Mattermost's own MCP server does: a display name beside the id is a second argument to keep in step with the first; an address is one argument, exact and readable at once.
  • A link as the destination of a write: one place has several links, and a link is read leniently; the address is the one form a write takes, so a refusal of every other form is simple to state and to act on.
  • Addresses for the writes that are the user's own: following a thread, saving a post or showing typing changes nothing others see, and gains nothing from a stricter argument.
  • Pick the most likely of several matches: The likeliest channel is still a guess, and a post in the wrong channel cannot be taken back unseen.
  • Search for tools before loading them: Mattermost's own agent finds tools with a search tool inside its plugin. Every client mm-mcp serves loads the catalogue itself; revisit when the catalogue outgrows that.
  • Leave bots out of lists unless asked: Each user says whether it is a bot, which a model reads as easily, and a bot is sometimes what the person is looking for.
  • Links made from ids: Mattermost opens /<team>/channels/<id> too, but a person reads nothing in it, and a direct message's id is the conversation, which is the link a model wrongly gave for a post.
  • Only /_redirect/pl/<id> for a post: it works without a team, and reads as internal; it is kept for a post whose team is not known.
  • A direct message's link in the team an answer is about: the same conversation would have a different link in each answer, and an answer about several teams has no one team.
  • A team's link on every post and channel: the channel's link holds the team, and a link repeated on every post costs every answer; a team's link comes with the team itself.
  • A tool that turns a link into an id: every id argument takes the link, so the model needs no extra call.
  • Take a link to another server by its names: a channel or team of the same name here is not the one the person meant, and a post there is not one here.
  • Ids only: A model that passed a channel's name to read_channel got Mattermost's "invalid channel_id" and had to find the id first; an ambiguous name is refused all the same, so taking a name guesses nothing.

docs.title: ADR-031: A message is checked before it is posted, and says it was written with AI
docs.text:
Every tool that takes a message the model wrote checks it before it acts, and before the person is asked where mm-mcp asks (ADR-033): create_post, dm, group_message, update_post and propose_post. A message longer than the server takes, by the MaxPostSize it tells its clients, is refused with its length and the limit, so the model shortens it, splits it into replies, or attaches the full text as a file. Its mentions are found as Mattermost finds them: Mattermost's own Markdown parser reads the message, so code of any kind mentions nobody, and its words are split and their trailing punctuation tried off as the server does, so @here. at the end of a sentence is @here and _@channel_ is @channel. Every mention of a person is resolved against the server's users: one nobody has is refused with the closest usernames, and a deactivated user is named in the question where mm-mcp asks, since they will not be notified. @channel, @all and @here are spelled out in it with how many people they reach. An edit notifies nobody, Mattermost's own rule, so update_post checks its length and none of its mentions, and says so. Where mm-mcp asks, the question puts what a post does, its mentions, files and marker, before the message, which it shows exactly as it will be posted.

Every post and edit the model writes carries Mattermost's own ai_generated_by property, set to the user it was written for, which Mattermost's web app shows as AI-generated beside the post's time. Mattermost accepts the property only for the poster or a bot, so it says who the post is from and that a model wrote it, nothing more. An edit sends the post's properties back with the marker only when the post holds no others: Mattermost sanitises the properties an edit sends, and in its hardened mode refuses some, so a post carrying an integration's properties is edited unmarked. Where mm-mcp asks, its question says whether the post will be marked. MM_MCP_MARK_AI_GENERATED=false turns the marker off; it is on unless turned off. A draft is not marked: the person sends it, after changing it as they like.

The server's own instructions tell the model how Mattermost renders a message, in a few lines every session reads once, rather than every tool's description repeating it.

A colleague reads a post as the person's own words, so what reaches them should be what was meant, and say plainly when a model wrote it. A mention that names nobody notifies nobody and reads as a mistake; a mention of everyone notifies everyone, which whoever approves the call should see in it. A message Mattermost would refuse is better refused before anyone spends attention on it.

A write others see states in its call what it does to them, as values mm-mcp reads itself, checked before the call goes further and again just before the write, so a call made on an outdated reading is refused. They are in the call's arguments because that is what a client's own approval shows, a person's prompt or an AI reviewer's, and the model cannot state them without reading the place first. A missing or wrong value is refused with the real one and where it comes from, and the refusal asks the model to weigh whether that is what the person meant.

create_post states how far its message goes. reaches is the channel's member count, on every post: everyone in the channel can read it, whatever it mentions. notifies is required exactly where Mattermost's web app asks before sending, with the number it shows: every member but the sender for @channel, @all or @here in a channel of more than 5 members, while the server's EnableConfirmNotificationsToChannel is on and the person has use_channel_mentions there; otherwise the members in the channel of the largest user group mentioned, above 5, that the person may mention. The 5 is the web app's own NOTIFY_ALL_MEMBERS, which the server does not publish; the rest is read from the server.

update_post states reaches as well, and never notifies, since an edit reaches everyone the post does and notifies nobody. It states the post's current text in full, old_message, alongside message, its replacement: the model holds all of what it replaces, and the client's approval shows both texts. An old_message that differs from the post's current text, because the post changed after the model read it or because only part of it is quoted, is refused with the current text. A post with reactions, or with replies in the thread it starts, also takes responses, their number, as read_post gives it. An edit leaves those responses under the replacing text and tells nobody, so a reaction given to one sentence stands under another; the refusal names who responded, and that a reply in the thread may carry the change better.

A deletion states how much goes: delete_draft states discards, the draft's characters, as list_drafts gives its length; delete_post states deletes, the post and every reply in its thread, other people's included. A refusal quotes what would go.

docs.title: Not chosen
docs.text:
• Split an overlong message into replies on the tool's own initiative: One call would make several posts; the model can split it, and each part is then a call of its own.
  • Leave the AI marker to the model: It would be set inconsistently, and a post's provenance is not the model's to decide.
  • Mark drafts: The person writes the last version of a draft and sends it themselves, a proposal of mm-mcp's included (ADR-035).
  • Formatting guidance in every tool's description: It would cost every tool listing in every session for what one paragraph of the server's instructions says.
  • An acknowledgement the model sets, such as target_audience_ack: The model sets it without looking; a value it must read, and that mm-mcp reads too, it cannot.
  • reaches only above a threshold: A number to choose, configure and explain, where the count is one read and a refusal hands it over.
  • One number for both: A message reaches the whole channel whatever it mentions, and only some messages alert everyone at once; Mattermost asks about the second alone.
  • An edit time or another version, to bind a call to what the model read: It means nothing in a prompt; a draft's length catches all but a rewrite of the same length, and the full current text an edit states catches every change.
  • A count of the characters an edit replaces: The model counts, or copies the count from a refusal without thinking, and an edit replaces all of a post's text, so the count tells an addition from a rewrite no better than nothing.
  • Only the changed part of a post, with its replacement: A change in two places of three takes a long part or several calls, and the model does not hold the whole post.
  • A label the model gives its edit, such as addition or rewrite: The model grading its own work, against a threshold between a correction and a rewrite nobody could justify.

docs.title: ADR-032: Every list pages by an opaque cursor, to its end
docs.text:
Every tool that answers with a list takes limit and cursor, and answers with next_cursor, which is absent on the last page. The model passes next_cursor back as cursor, with the same other arguments, for the next page; a different limit is fine. This is MCP's own way of paging its lists, so a model that has paged resources has paged these. A list's limit has a small default and a hard maximum, and a list bounded by its input, such as get_users with the names it is given, or by the tool itself, such as the checks diagnose makes, is the one exception. TestEveryListPagesByCursor holds every tool that answers with a list to this.

A cursor is opaque: base64 of the tool's name, a fingerprint of the arguments that chose the list, and where to continue. A cursor from another tool, or from the same tool with other arguments, is refused, so a model cannot continue the wrong list. Where to continue follows the list's Mattermost endpoint. A channel is read back or forward from a post, by before and after, which stays right while people post. Mattermost compares only times there, so a page that ended inside a millisecond would lose the rest of it: a page that more follow ends on a whole millisecond, cut back to before its last one, and the tool asks for one post more than the page holds to know whether it must. A millisecond with more posts than the page holds is read whole on a page larger than asked for, the one way a page exceeds its limit. Followed threads, which Mattermost pages by when they were last replied to, are read the same way. A thread is read on from a post and its time. Where Mattermost's own read has the same flaw and no way around it, the tool reads another way: the read around the last unread post leaves out the posts written in the first unread one's millisecond, so read_unread reads the posts written since the person last read the channel instead. A list Mattermost gives whole, such as a database search's answer or the user's channels, is cut into pages at an offset. A list Mattermost gives a page at a time, ordered by a value two items can share, such as a time to the millisecond, is read whole, each item once, and put in an order with a tiebreaker, so the pages the tool gives are the same however Mattermost settled the ties; an item tied across one of Mattermost's own page boundaries can still be missed by it, which the tool cannot see. Every order a tool pages through breaks ties by id, so the same arguments give the same pages.

A list reaches its end. Where Mattermost caps a list, the tool says so in its description: at most 1000 users for one search term, 50 public channels in a team for one channel search term, and the 100 most recent matches of a post or file search, which the answer marks capped when it reached them. Where Mattermost's answer is capped below what a list holds, the tool reads it another way: a read since a time that Mattermost answers with its most, 1000 changed posts, is read back from the newest instead, page by page, until it passes the time. Where the specification documents paging the router does not do, and the router pages by a parameter the specification leaves out, the tool sends what the router reads, declared as undocumented (ADR-028) and shown working by a live test past one of Mattermost's pages. Where Mattermost pages wrongly, as its saved posts take their page parameter as an offset in posts, the call says so and sends what works, and a live test counts the requests reading 205 items takes. A list is read until a page comes back empty rather than short, since Mattermost leaves out of a page, after counting it, posts the person may no longer read.

A model told "there may be more" with no way to fetch it stops at the first page or guesses; a list it can read to its end is one it can answer from. One way of paging across every tool is one thing to learn. A page boundary that skips an item is worse than no paging, since nothing tells the model an item is missing.

docs.title: Not chosen
docs.text:
• Expose Mattermost's own paging per tool: page numbers here, post ids there, and offsets that are page numbers; the model would learn each, and some of them skip items.
  • A truncated flag and a larger limit: The model can ask for more only up to the maximum, and nothing reaches past it.
  • A transparent cursor, such as a page number: A model would compute its own, for another list or past the end.

docs.title: ADR-033: The client decides whether a write runs, and mm-mcp enforces its own guards
docs.text:
Whether a write runs is the MCP client's to decide: its prompt, its permission rules, or its auto mode. mm-mcp does not ask the person by default. What it controls is what it enforces itself, on every call, whoever approved it:

  • It writes nothing until MM_MCP_ALLOW_WRITES is true (ADR-021).
  • A message is checked before it is posted, and each post and edit is marked as written with AI, on by default (ADR-031, ADR-034).
  • Each write others see states what it does to them, as values mm-mcp reads itself: how many people a post or an edit reaches and a post notifies, the full text an edit replaces and how many reactions and replies answer it, and how many characters or posts a deletion takes away (ADR-031). A missing or wrong value is refused with the real one, and the refusal tells the model to consider whether that is what the person meant before it calls again.
  • Each write others see names its places by address, matched exactly (ADR-030).
  • Each value is read again just before the write, so a call made on an outdated reading is refused: members who joined, a reply that arrived, a post edited or reacted to, or a draft typed on since the model read it.

The client's approval sees the tool's name and its arguments, and in Claude Code's auto mode nothing else, so what the write does to others is put in its arguments rather than in a question only some clients show.

MM_MCP_ELICITATION_OPT_IN, false by default, has mm-mcp ask as well. Each write others see then asks the person through MCP elicitation before it acts: what will be sent, where and under whose name, with one required checkbox and no default, so a client whose approvals are automatic cannot accept a form with no fields. The question is bound to the call's input and to what the call acts on, its fingerprint read again just before it acts, so an answer accepts only what the person was shown. A client that cannot show the question is refused with the error MCP defines for a missing client capability, and nothing is written. A refusal tells the model that either the person declined or their client answered without showing the question, and names propose_post and unsetting the setting as the ways forward. While the setting is on, the server's instructions and each such tool's description say the person is asked; otherwise they say mm-mcp does not ask and the client approves the call.

It is a convenience in a client that shows the question, not a safeguard. The answer reaches mm-mcp from the client, and mm-mcp cannot tell the person's answer from the client's. The Claude desktop app's Code tab and its VS Code extension decline the question unseen (mm-mcp#20; upstream anthropics/claude-code#89858 and #96043), Codex in Full Access accepts a form without fields on its own, Copilot CLI's Autopilot answers elicitations itself, about half the coding clients support none, and the 2026-07-28 revision lets a client gather the answer "from the user or other sources". Presenting such an answer as the safety mechanism would mislead anyone who does not know MCP well.

MM_MCP_FORCE_HUMAN_IN_THE_LOOP_IN_CLAUDE_CODE, false by default, marks each write others see with _meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"]: true. Claude Code then shows its own prompt on every call, in every permission mode, and no allow rule or "don't ask again" skips it. It is Claude Code's own mark, which no other client reads, so it is documented as a Claude Code feature, not a guarantee. With MM_MCP_ELICITATION_OPT_IN=true as well, the server stops at start with what to change: the person would be asked twice for one write.

MM_MCP_ASK_BEFORE_WRITES sets nothing. A server started with it set stops and names MM_MCP_ELICITATION_OPT_IN, so nobody believes a setting decides who asks when it does not. The server says at start who decides on a write.

Not every write has a person in the loop. An agent that works alone, such as a scheduled report, needs only to be allowed by the client's rules. That is why forcing a human in the loop is a setting of its own: a mark that overrides allow rules makes unattended writing impossible. A change that is the user's alone or gone in seconds never asks, whatever the settings (ADR-021), and neither does a press in a proposal's view, the person's own decision on what the view shows them; MM_MCP_POST_FROM_VIEWS takes Post out of the view for a client that cannot be trusted with it (ADR-035).

The names say what the person gets. "Elicitation opt-in" names the mechanism and that it is chosen, not assumed; "force human in the loop" names the outcome, a person on every call, overriding what the client would otherwise allow; and "in Claude Code" names the one client that enforces it. Each is a yes or no, and the one combination that contradicts itself is refused rather than resolved silently.

docs.title: Not chosen
docs.text:
• Asking by default, as the safety mechanism: An answer through the protocol is no proof a person saw anything, and in the client that answers unseen nothing could be written at all.
  • A step that has the model check its own plan, or an acknowledgement it sets: Such as answering ABORT or CONFIRMED, or target_audience_ack (mm-mcp#42): the model grading its own work, where a value mm-mcp reads cannot be stated without looking.
  • One setting with three values: Values naming who asks, such as mm-mcp or client, read as something to install or connect rather than as a choice.
  • The mark on every write by default: It overrides allow rules, so no agent could write unattended.
  • The mark while mm-mcp asks too: The person would be asked twice for one post, wearing out the attention a question depends on.
  • Detect the client and stop asking it: A client's name says nothing reliable about whether it shows questions, and the same client behaves differently from one mode to another.
  • Start with MM_MCP_ASK_BEFORE_WRITES set, ignoring it: Whoever set it would believe it decides who asks.

docs.title: ADR-034: Agents are let in visibly, not kept out
docs.text:
mm-mcp holds that the safe way for an agent to reach Mattermost is a proper way in that the server can see, and says so to administrators. It asks them for Mattermost's own OAuth, through one public app they register or dynamic client registration, and it keeps what makes it visible on by default: each post and edit marked as written with AI, what each write others see does stated and checked (ADR-033), and User-Agent: mm-mcp/<version> on every request it sends, its login's included. Where the proper way in is open, it is the only way mm-mcp login tries on its own, and the others are used only when the person names one; where it is closed, mm-mcp login still logs the person in, through a browser window of its own, Playwright's Chromium or a pasted token (ADR-019), and the documentation says plainly what that means for the administrator's policy rather than presenting it as neutral.

The reason is that a policy cannot keep agents out any more. An agent with computer use or a browser extension opens Mattermost where the person is already logged in, and reads and types as them. Switching personal access tokens off, forbidding remote debugging, or requiring a managed device stops none of that. What a policy does decide is the way an agent comes in: through the person's browser it sees whatever is on the screen, posts unmarked, asks nobody, and cannot be told apart or ended without ending the person's own session; through mm-mcp it reaches Mattermost's API alone, is read-only until writes are allowed, states and checks what each post does to others, marks them, names itself, and holds one session that can be ended on its own. Closing the proper ways in does not keep the agent out; it moves it to the way nobody can see.

This does not satisfy every security policy, and the documentation does not claim it does; the For administrators page makes the case. A change that makes mm-mcp harder for a server to recognise, such as a default that leaves posts unmarked or requests unnamed, goes against this record.

docs.title: Not chosen
docs.text:
• Refusing to log in where personal access tokens are off: It honours the policy on paper while the agent goes through the browser instead, unseen.
  • Offering the other ways in without saying what they mean for policy: The administrator who has to decide would find out from the people who used them, not from mm-mcp.
  • Leaving visibility to settings that are off by default: A mark or a name that most people never turn on does not let a server recognise the agent.

docs.title: ADR-035: A proposed post waits as the person's draft, for them to send
docs.text:
propose_post lets the person post what the model proposes. It checks the message as a post is checked (ADR-031) and saves it as the person's Mattermost draft where it would go: a channel, a thread, or a direct or group message the person already has. A conversation that does not exist yet is not started: creating its channel puts it in the other people's sidebar at once, an empty conversation they see, so the first message in one goes through dm or group_message. The draft is the vessel. Mattermost keeps it in the message box and the drafts list of every client, so a proposal outlives the conversation and the view. In a client that renders views, the view shows the draft as it will be posted, with Post, Edit and Discard (ADR-022). In one that renders none, the answer links the place where the draft waits, for the person to send it from Mattermost.

Pressing Post in the view sends the draft as the view shows it, marked as written with AI (ADR-031). It is a convenience where the client renders the view, not proof the person pressed it: mm-mcp cannot tell a click from a script. The press goes through the writing tool only views call (ADR-022), which the client keeps from its model, and names the text the view shows. mm-mcp acts only on what a view put in the draft, mm-mcp's proposal or the person's text from the view's editor, unchanged, and only while it holds that text and nothing the person added in Mattermost, so a press never sends text the person did not see, nor words they wrote in Mattermost and have not sent. A newer proposal refuses the press, and the view draws it as it is now; a draft the person typed on, or gave files or settings, in Mattermost is sent from there. The message is checked again at the press. Posting deletes the draft, so a second press finds nothing. Edit writes into the draft, and Discard deletes it, each bound in the same way. Replace mine acts only while the person's draft holds what the view shows of it. A message Mattermost has its sender confirm, one whose @channel, @all, @here or user group alerts more than five people, is posted only on a second press: the first answers with Mattermost's counts, read at the press, and the view asks, as Mattermost would. The model learns what the person did from Mattermost, the draft gone or the post in the channel, and, where the client passes it on, from the view's update of its context in mm-mcp's fixed words, with the text quoted as data.

The view hides nothing that is sent. A link shows where it leads where its text says otherwise, characters the eye cannot see or that turn the text's direction are counted and flagged, and the text as written, each such character shown by its code point, is a click away.

mm-mcp writes over the person's own words only on their action, or by a call that states what it discards (ADR-031). A draft that holds mm-mcp's own earlier proposal, unchanged, is mm-mcp's to replace. Once the person has typed in it, it is theirs, and so is a draft they changed with Edit in the view. A proposal carries a mark of its text in the draft's properties, and a draft changed with Edit a mark of the person's text, which the view's presses reach: a draft whose text no longer matches its mark, or that has none, or that holds files or settings the person added, is the person's. propose_post never replaces one, and where the person's own draft already holds the proposed text, the view asks them as it does over any draft of theirs. In a client that renders views, a proposal where the person's draft waits is not written: the view shows their draft beside it, or, when the model says the person asked to change their draft (revises_draft), the proposal as a revision of it, word by word, with Replace mine, or Apply, and Keep mine. Without a view, the call is refused with what the draft holds and the ways on: they finish or clear it in Mattermost, the model posts with create_post, or, when they asked for their draft to be changed, the model deletes it with delete_draft, whose call states what it discards and which asks where mm-mcp asks, and proposes again.

A proposal carries no AI marker. Mattermost's own client sends a draft's properties with the post, so the marker would travel, but what the person sends from Mattermost is theirs (ADR-031). The mark of a proposal's text travels the same way, where nothing shows it.

The client is trusted to keep the tools only views call from its model, and to press only when the person clicks; mm-mcp cannot tell a click from a script. A press never asks, as no call from a view does (ADR-022), and changes what it changes as the person's own action (ADR-021, ADR-033). MM_MCP_POST_FROM_VIEWS, true by default, is the lever for a client that cannot be trusted with that: false takes Post out of the view, refuses a press on it, and the draft waits in Mattermost for the person to send.

A proposal lets the person decide on the text in the conversation without a question their client might answer unseen (ADR-033), and leaves them a draft in Mattermost whatever their client renders.

docs.title: Not chosen
docs.text:
• A token in the result, single-use and bound to the text: Every part of a result reaches some client's model (ADR-022), and a token fetched from a tool only views call protects nothing that keeping that tool from the model does not.
  • The draft's update time, to bind a press: The text the view shows is what the person agreed to send. A time would refuse a draft typed on and typed back, and would have to travel in the answer for the view alone.
  • The confirmation's counts in the proposal: An edit in the view changes what the message mentions, and members join; counted at the press, they are Mattermost's as it sends.
  • Post through create_post: Its checks are a post's, and the question it asks where mm-mcp is set to ask is shown by no client during a call from a view.
  • Ask again after the press, as a setting: For the same reason; the setting takes Post away instead.
  • A view that expires after a few minutes: The text a press names already refuses a stale press, and a person who reopens a conversation and presses Post on an unchanged draft sends what they see.
  • Set the person's draft aside and restore it once the proposal is posted: Until then every client of theirs shows the model's text where their words were, and if mm-mcp stops, or they type in that box, their draft is lost.
  • Replace the person's draft on a call that states its length: A tool that does not ask may not destroy anything (ADR-021), and one that asks is refused in a client that cannot show the question, which is where a proposal is needed most; delete_draft states the length and asks where mm-mcp asks, and the proposal follows it.
  • Files in a proposal: A draft holds only files already uploaded, so a proposal with files would send them to Mattermost before the person agreed; a post with files goes through create_post, whose call names them.

docs.title: ADR-036: Real clients run the views at pinned versions, with a scripted model
docs.text:
The views are tested in the clients people use, not only in the official MCP Apps bridge (ADR-022). Goose's desktop app and VS Code each start mm-mcp over stdio against the live instance, draw its views, and are driven as a person would drive them, on every pull request, in the Client Tests job that CI Complete requires. A client's behaviour is what the views depend on and what the specification leaves open: where a view's data reaches the model, whether a view's call is allowed, what a client does with the tool only views call. The spike (mm-mcp#37) found each of those by driving these two clients by machine, and these tests keep finding them.

  • Pinned versions. .github/tool-versions.env pins each client, and go run ./tools/clients install, which task test:clients runs first, unpacks the pinned release under .tmp/clients/, checked against the SHA-256 its publisher gives: GitHub's digest of a Goose release asset, VS Code's update service's. A failure on a pull request is then the change's, never a client's new release. The tests find an installed client and fail naming the task when it is missing (ADR-009).
  • A scripted model. Each client's model is internal/scriptedmodel, an OpenAI-compatible endpoint the test serves on the loopback address. A message SCRIPT <tool> <json> is answered with that tool's call, a tool's result with Done, so the client calls mm-mcp exactly as the test says, at no cost, the same way every time. Goose reaches it as an OpenAI provider; VS Code through a development extension, tests/live/clients/vscode-model, that offers it as a chat model. The model keeps every request, so a test sees which tools the client put in front of it.
  • Driven over CDP. Each client starts with a remote debugging port, and tests/live/clients/driver.mjs types, clicks and reads through Playwright's connectOverCDP, one command a run, printing what it found as JSON. The Go tests, in tests/live under the live and clients tags, seed Mattermost, start the client with a configuration of its own, and decide what each answer means. Every wait is on a condition with a deadline. A failure keeps a screenshot and the logs of the client and of mm-mcp in .tmp/clients-artifacts, which CI uploads.
  • Each client set apart. Goose takes its configuration, data and state from GOOSE_PATH_ROOT, and VS Code its settings and mcp.json from its own user data directory, both in the test's temporary folder, so a run never touches the person's own. mm-mcp is started through a wrapper that holds its configuration, since Goose's desktop app passes on no environment of its own. VS Code starts with --password-store=basic, since without a keyring it shows a native dialog no debugging client can see, and its MCP server waits on it.
  • Where it runs. CI runs the tests on Linux under Xvfb, and task test:clients starts a virtual display there itself when none is set. Elsewhere the clients draw on the screen of whoever runs the task.

A client that changes what the views rely on fails a pull request only once its pin moves, in a change of its own. Dependabot does not follow these clients, so the Client Drift workflow does, daily: go run ./tools/clients bump moves the pins to each client's newest release, and the client tests run on them. When they pass, it opens or updates one pull request that moves the pins, starts CI on its branch, since a pull request a workflow opens triggers none of its own, and closes an issue about releases that failed before. When they fail, it opens one issue naming the releases tried, or comments on the one already open, with the run that holds the screenshot and the logs. Releases already proposed in the open pull request, or last reported in the open issue, are not tried again, so a day without a new release does nothing, and a failure is reported once a release rather than every day; a run started by hand can try them again.

docs.title: Not chosen
docs.text:
• Inference from a real model: It costs money on every pull request, needs an account and a secret that a pull request from a fork cannot have, and answers differently from one run to the next. What a model decides with the tools is not measured here (ADR-037).
  • The newest client on every pull request: A client's release would fail every pull request open on the day it ships, for a reason none of them caused.
  • An issue per client that moved: When both clients moved and the tests fail, the issue would blame both; one issue names the releases tried, and the run names the test that failed.
  • Launching the client through Playwright's Electron support: Launching the packaged apps that way timed out in the spike; a debugging port works for both.
  • Driving the clients from Go over CDP: A view lives in frames inside other frames, in other processes, which Playwright follows and a hand-written client would have to.
  • A stand-in client of mm-mcp's own: It would share mm-mcp's reading of the specification, as a fake Mattermost would share its reading of the API (ADR-005); the official bridge is the reference, and real clients are what people run.
  • Checksums kept in the repository: Each publisher gives the SHA-256 of what it ships, read over TLS from the same place as the version; a second copy to move with every pin would only fall out of step.

docs.title: ADR-037: The views are tested in the bridge, in real clients, and by hand
docs.text:
mm-mcp's views (ADR-022) are tested at three levels, each where it can be relied on. A check that gates a merge involves no inference and no closed-source client.

  1. The page against the specification. The view page runs in headless Chromium inside the official MCP Apps bridge, @modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/app-bridge, the specification authors' own host side, with made-up data, on every pull request: the View Tests job, which CI Complete requires (task test:views). It holds the handshake, what reaches the page and what it sends, every press and what the page does with the answer, and that the page acts only on a click and never speaks for the person. A host of mm-mcp's own would share mm-mcp's reading of the specification, as a fake Mattermost would share its reading of the API (ADR-005).
  2. Real clients that can be driven. Goose's desktop app and VS Code, at the versions the repository pins, draw the views against the live instance with a scripted model, on every pull request, and a daily run tries each client's newest release (ADR-036).
  3. Apps no machine can drive. Claude desktop, Claude on the web, and other apps whose source is closed are checked by a person before a release that changes the views, with the Client check issue form, which asks what the client tests ask and keeps the app's MCP logs as the record. These apps offer no automation interface, take no model but their own, and need a signed-in, paid account; driving their screens would put inference and an account into CI. This level stays a check by hand.

What a model does with the tools is not measured. Whether a model calls show when the person asks to see something, or propose_post when they should have the last word, depends on the model. A measure worth having runs many models of many sizes, many times over, at a cost an open-source project does not carry. The server's instructions and each tool's description say what the tool is for. An organisation that deploys mm-mcp with a model of its choice can measure how that model uses them. ADR-014 says what the gates measure.

docs.title: Not chosen
docs.text:
• Scheduled evals with one model through its API: One model's choices say little about another's, and the people who run mm-mcp choose their own; a measure across models of every size costs more than this project carries.
  • Driving the closed-source apps' screens: It needs inference and a paid account in CI, and breaks on every change of their interface.
  • Every level on every pull request: The apps a person checks by hand are checked when the views change, before a release, rather than holding up every change.
